name: Royal Docks Loop
blurb: Out on Cycleway 3 through Cable Street, Limehouse and Poplar to the Royal Docks, back up the River Lea to Three Mills and Abbey Mills, then home by Mile End, Whitechapel and Hoxton. Spies, Soviet jewels, a siege and the sewer that saved London.
card_blurb: Out on Cycleway 3 through Cable Street and Poplar to the Royal Docks, back up the River Lea and home through the East End.

legs.name: Out: Cable Street and the docks
Back: the Lea and the East End

stops.name: Bunhill Fields
stops.note: Go in by the City Road gate and walk to the middle of the broad path. The tall white obelisk is Defoe's; Bunyan and Blake are a few steps away.

stories.title: The double life of Daniel Defoe
paras: Find the tall white obelisk in the middle of the burial ground. Daniel De Foe, it says, author of Robinson Crusoe. It says nothing about his other trade.

It is the summer of 1703. Defoe, a merchant and a dissenter, has written a satire that has gone badly wrong. The Shortest Way with the Dissenters pretends to call for people like him to be crushed. Once the authorities know who wrote it, they put a price on his head.

On the twenty ninth, thirtieth and thirty first of July he stands in the pillory, an hour a day. The crowd is supposed to pelt him. Instead, the story goes, they throw flowers and drink his health. Then he goes back to Newgate.
Robert Harley, Speaker of the Commons and soon Secretary of State, pays his fine out of secret service money. In November Defoe walks free, and from now on he works for Harley.

In the autumn of 1706 Harley sends him to Edinburgh, where the Scottish Parliament is arguing over union with England. Defoe lets it be known he has fled his creditors, makes friends on every side, reports on them all to London and writes for the union. In January 1707 the Scots vote it through.

When the Whigs take power he simply changes masters. By 1717 he is helping to run a Jacobite paper while telling the government he is drawing its teeth. Some scholars think he was fooling his paymasters too.
He dies in April 1731 in Ropemakers Alley, near Moorgate, probably hiding from creditors.

stops.name: Soviet House, Moorgate
stops.note: Stop by number 49 Moorgate, on the west side, about two hundred metres south of Moorgate station. Whatever building you see, this is the address the police came to in 1927.

stories.title: The raid that blinded the codebreakers
paras: Number 49 Moorgate. In 1927 they call it Soviet House. It holds Arcos, the company that runs Soviet trade with Britain, and the Soviet trade delegation, which claims diplomatic immunity.

At about twenty past four on the twelfth of May, the police come in. They take over the telephone exchange and hold every member of staff. They want one thing: a secret War Office document which, an informer says, was copied here on a photostat machine. The Home Secretary, Sir William Joynson-Hicks, is sure of it.
In a cipher room with no handle on the door they find a clerk, Anton Miller, burning papers. There is a struggle. A list falls from his pocket: cover addresses for communists across the world.
The search goes on for days. Safes are drilled open. But the document is not there. The government cannot hide it, and has to admit as much in the Commons.

So on the twenty fourth of May Baldwin reaches for something else. He reads out secret Soviet telegrams, sent to and from Moscow. None of this came from Moorgate. It came from British codebreakers, who have been reading Soviet cipher for years.

Within days Britain breaks off relations with Moscow. The codebreakers pay the price. Moscow moves its secrets to one time pads, which cannot be broken when used properly, and its top level diplomatic traffic goes dark for the rest of the years between the wars.
The raid found little that London did not already know. It gave away the one secret that mattered.

stops.name: Cable Street
stops.note: Stand across the road from St George's Town Hall, 236 Cable Street, where the whole mural fits in view. The cycle track runs right past it.

stories.title: The day the march turned back
paras: Look up at the mural on the old town hall. Mounted police, a lorry on its side, raised fists, a woman at a window with a chamber pot. It shows one Sunday afternoon on this street.

It is the fourth of October 1936. Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists means to march through the East End, home to tens of thousands of Jewish families. The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Labour Party tell people to stay away. The East End does not listen.

By mid afternoon two or three thousand Blackshirts are drawn up in Royal Mint Street, the street you have just ridden along. Thousands of police are there to clear their way. Against them stand at least a hundred thousand people.

At Aldgate the crowd is too dense to move, so the police try Cable Street. They meet a lorry turned over by Christian Street, and more barricades behind it. Women at upstairs windows throw whatever comes to hand. All day the shout, borrowed from Spain, is they shall not pass.
The Commissioner of Police, Sir Philip Game, tells Mosley the march cannot go on. The Blackshirts turn about and march west instead. About a hundred and fifty people are arrested.

Two days later, in Berlin, Mosley secretly marries Diana Mitford in the drawing room of Joseph Goebbels, with Hitler among the guests. Before the year is out Parliament bans political uniforms. In 1940, on the advice of MI5, Mosley is locked up without trial.
The Blackshirts never did march down Cable Street.

stops.name: Poplar
stops.note: Go in by the park gate on Woodstock Terrace and walk about sixty metres west to the angel memorial. The children's names and ages are cut into its sides.

stories.title: The school in Upper North Street
paras: Look up at the angel with her wings spread. Then walk round and read the names and ages on the sides.

It is the morning of the thirteenth of June 1917, a Wednesday. Just before half past eleven Londoners look up and see something new: a formation of big biplanes, flying in broad daylight. They are Gothas, fourteen of them, from airfields near Ghent, led by Captain Ernst Brandenburg. Until now the raiders came at night, in airships. This is the first time a squadron of aeroplanes has come for London.

Most of the bombs fall around Liverpool Street. On the way home one Gotha drops a fifty kilo bomb on the council school in Upper North Street, a few hundred yards from here. It goes through the roof, through the girls' classroom at the top, through the boys' classroom below, and explodes on the ground floor, among sixty four infants.
Eighteen children die, sixteen of them five or six years old. The caretaker, Benjamin Batt, digs in the rubble and finds his own son.

The raid kills a hundred and sixty two people, more than any other raid on London in the war. There is no warning. London has no warning system. The fury that follows helps bring about something new: in April 1918, the Royal Air Force.
Fifteen of the children are buried together in one grave. Poplar pays for this memorial by public subscription. It is unveiled in June 1919 by the general who commanded London's air defences.

stories.title: The Russian jewels
paras: In 1920 the most famous man in Poplar is George Lansbury, its first Labour mayor. He edits the Daily Herald, the only daily paper on the side of the Labour movement. It fights any British war on Soviet Russia, and it is always short of money.
Early that year he meets Lenin in Moscow. That summer a Soviet delegation comes to London, and in August Lev Kamenev takes its lead.

What the Russians do not know is that the government's codebreakers have been reading their cipher telegrams home since May. In August some of them are given to the newspapers. They show Moscow offering money to the Daily Herald. Within weeks the papers find where it comes from: Russian jewels, sold in London.

Lansbury has sworn in print the Herald has taken no Bolshevik money. He believes it. But one of his directors, the publisher Francis Meynell, has been bringing it in. His MI5 file says he smuggled diamonds in a box of chocolate creams. Lansbury's son Edgar helps turn jewels into banknotes.
The offer comes to seventy five thousand pounds. Lansbury asks his readers, and the directors say no. Kamenev is asked to leave the country.

A year later Lansbury goes to prison anyway. Poor relief comes from local rates, so the poorest boroughs pay most. In 1921 Poplar's council refuses to hand on its share for London's common services. Thirty councillors march to the High Court behind a band and are jailed, the men in Brixton, the women in Holloway. After six weeks they walk free, and the law is changed.

stops.name: East India Dock Basin
stops.note: Stand by the water of the basin. The basin, its lock out to the river and the old wall along the road are what is left of the East India Company's dock. The settlers' memorial is about three hundred metres west, on the river at Virginia Quay.

stories.title: The Jolly George
paras: Picture a small steamer in the docks behind you, taking on cargo. Her name is the Jolly George. She is bound for Danzig.

It is May 1920. Russia is at war again, this time with the new Poland, and Polish troops have just marched into Kiev. Britain is not at war. But the crates going into her hold are marked O H M S, Munitions for Poland. Inside are eighteen pounder field guns and their shells.

The dockers can read. Plenty of them want no part in a war on the Russian revolution. For weeks a young boilermaker named Harry Pollitt, of the Hands Off Russia campaign, has been working the East End docks with one message: do not load the guns.
On the tenth of May the men refuse. The coal heavers will not fuel the ship. A deputation goes to the union, and its leaders, Ernest Bevin among them, promise to back them.
The owners give in. The guns come back out of the hold, and on the fifteenth of May the Jolly George sails without them.

It is one small strike. But in August, when Britain seems ready to go to war for Poland, the unions and the Labour Party threaten a national strike, and councils of action spring up across the country. There is no war.

Fifty years later the Soviet Union puts the story on a postage stamp: Harry Pollitt, who went on to lead the British Communist Party for a quarter of a century, and a little ship called the Jolly George.

stories.title: The Company's dock
paras: Long before there was a dock here, this was Blackwall: a scrap of firm shore at the edge of the marshes, where ships could lie below the great bend of the river.

On the twentieth of December 1606 three small ships drop down the river from here: the Susan Constant, the Godspeed and the Discovery, under Captain Christopher Newport. On board are about a hundred and five men and boys, sent by the Virginia Company to plant a colony in America. One of them, a soldier called John Smith, spends much of the voyage under arrest, accused of plotting to make himself king.

In May 1607 they choose a marshy island in a Virginia river and call it Jamestown. By the next January only thirty eight of them are alive. But the colony holds. It is the first English settlement in America that lasts.

Two centuries later the most powerful trading company in the world builds its own dock on this spot. The East India Company's dock opens in 1806, behind high walls, for the great East Indiamen of a thousand tons and more, home from India and China with tea, spices, indigo and silk.
In 1967 the East India Docks are the first of London's docks to close. Most of them lie under offices now. This basin and the old wall are what is left, and the mud belongs to the wading birds.

stops.name: Royal Victoria Dock
stops.note: Stop at the west end of the north quay. The old cranes and ExCeL run along the quay ahead. Across the water to the south east are the Millennium Mills, and planes leave London City Airport to the east.

stories.title: The dock on the marsh
paras: Look at the old cranes, and across the water. Every acre of it was dug out of a marsh.

In 1853 this is Plaistow Marshes, grazing and ditches below high tide. Then come the railway men. The engineer George Parker Bidder and the contractors Samuel Peto, Thomas Brassey and Edward Betts have built railways across the world, and they can see what is coming. Steamships, big ones, and they will need a railway at the quayside.

The Victoria Dock opens in 1855. It is London's first dock built for large steamships, the first joined directly to the railway network, and the first worked by hydraulic power. Its lock gates open in a minute and a half. A hydraulic capstan lets one man haul a rope that once took forty.

Ships bring tobacco, grain, wool and frozen meat from Australia, New Zealand and South America. Flour mills rise on the south side. When the Albert Dock opens next door in 1880, this one becomes the Royal Victoria.

Then comes the seventh of September 1940, a sunny Saturday. That afternoon some three hundred and fifty German bombers and six hundred fighters come up the Thames. The docks are the target. Timber and flour mills burn, ships sink, rum barrels burst in the heat. Silvertown, across the water, is a sea of fire, and the Woolwich ferry carries its people out all night. More than four hundred Londoners die by morning. The Blitz has begun.
The dock outlives the war. The last ships leave in 1981.

stories.title: Silvertown, 1917
paras: Look across to the great pale block of the Millennium Mills. A hundred yards from the mill on that spot stood a chemical works owned by Brunner Mond.
In 1915 the government needs explosives. So this works, among crowded streets, is turned over to purifying TNT. The company does not want the job. The ministry insists.

It is Friday the nineteenth of January 1917, early evening. On an upper floor of the works a fire breaks out where TNT is being melted. The chief chemist, Andrea Angel, is among the men fighting it. Firemen run over from the station across the road.
At about eight minutes to seven, some fifty tons of TNT go up at once.

The works vanishes. So do the fire station, two of the firemen and whole streets of houses. The mill is wrecked. Across the river a gasholder bursts into a fireball. The glow is seen in Guildford, and the blast is heard as far away as Norfolk.
Seventy three people are killed, Angel among them. More than four hundred are hurt.

London decides it must be a German spy, or a Zeppelin. No airship is seen anywhere that night. The inquiry finds no enemy hand, and the German records have never shown one. It blames the place itself: TNT should never have been worked in a crowded street. But the report stays secret until the 1950s, and the sabotage stories never quite die.

stops.name: Three Mills
stops.note: Stand on the bridge by the House Mill, the tall brick building over the water. The Clock Mill with its little clock tower is opposite; the old distillery buildings around them are now film studios.

stories.title: Gin, maize and a chemist from Motal
paras: The tall brick building on the water is the House Mill, built in 1776 to grind grain with the tide. From 1872 these mills belonged to J and W Nicholson, gin distillers.
It is 1915, and Britain is running short of acetone. The guns are fired with cordite, and cordite cannot be made without it.

The answer comes from a chemistry lecturer in Manchester. Chaim Weizmann was born in 1874 in Motal, a small Jewish town in the Russian Empire, now in Belarus. He has found a bacterium that eats the starch in maize and gives off acetone.

By his own account Winston Churchill, at the Admiralty, asks him for thirty thousand tons. So the government gives him this distillery to prove the process at scale. Here, among the gin stills, the first big fermentations run. Stray bacteria spoil batches, but the method holds and moves on to factories in Dorset, King's Lynn and Toronto.

Lloyd George, Minister of Munitions, later told a famous story in his memoirs: that the Balfour Declaration of 1917, Britain's promise of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, was Weizmann's reward for the acetone.
Treat that as a legend. The Declaration had many causes, and Weizmann had been arguing his case with ministers for years. The acetone opened doors. It did not write the letter.
In 1949 the boy from Motal became the first President of Israel.

stops.name: Abbey Mills
stops.note: Stop on the Greenway where it passes above the pumping station. The domed building below you to the south is the station of 1868; the silver one beyond it is its successor of 1997.

stories.title: The river that stank
paras: Look down at the gravel under your wheels. You are riding on a sewer. Inside this bank the waste of north London flows east to Beckton, as it has since the 1860s.

It is the summer of 1858, and the Thames is an open drain. Every flushing toilet in London empties into it, and the tide carries the filth up and down past Westminster. Then the heat comes. The newspapers call it the Great Stink.
In the new Houses of Parliament the curtains on the river side are soaked in chloride of lime. It does not help. Disraeli brings in a bill, and by the second of August it is law.

The engineer is Joseph Bazalgette. His plan: catch the sewage before it reaches the river, in great brick tunnels across the slope of London, and carry it far downstream. Eighty two miles of main sewers. Eleven hundred miles of street sewers. Three hundred and eighteen million bricks.

Now look at the domes below: Abbey Mills, finished in 1868. The sewage arrives deep underground, and eight great beam engines lift it into this bank, to run on to the outfall by gravity. The architect, Charles Driver, dressed it like a church, with a lantern, coloured ironwork and two Moorish chimneys. Londoners call it the Cathedral of Sewage. The chimneys came down in 1941, for fear a bomb would topple them.
Ride on west. Under your wheels, half of London is flowing the other way, out towards the sea.

stops.name: Mile End, Grove Road bridge
stops.note: Stop at the corner of Lichfield Road and Grove Road. The railway bridge fifty metres to your right carries the blue plaque. Roll up to read it if you like, then come back to this corner.

stories.title: The first flying bomb
paras: Find the blue plaque on the bridge. It names nobody. It says only that the first flying bomb on London fell here.

It is about twenty five past four in the morning, the thirteenth of June 1944, one week after D Day. A small pilotless aircraft comes in from France, its engine rasping like a motorbike. Over Grove Road the engine cuts out. Silence. Then it falls.
The blast wrecks the bridge and the houses beside it. Six people are killed, dozens hurt, about two hundred left homeless.
The Germans cannot see where their bombs land, so they ask their spies in Britain. Every one of them works for MI5.

Three days later Juan Pujol, the Spaniard known as Garbo, is asked for the times and places of the hits. So are Brutus and Tate. Later Eddie Chapman, the safecracker called Zigzag, gets the same job. Their handlers see a chance. Report the hits in north and west London, stay vague on times, and let the Germans think they are overshooting. If they shorten their aim, the bombs fall short of the centre.
It is a terrible sum: fewer deaths overall, more in some streets. The War Cabinet will not approve it. An official, Sir Findlater Stewart, starts it anyway, and Churchill backs him.

Did it work? The German commander had radio data showing his bombs falling short, and trusted the agents instead. How much they really moved the bombs, nobody can measure. One later reckoning is that, had he trusted the radio, the dead might have been half as many again.

stops.name: Sidney Street
stops.note: Stop on Sidney Street by Wexford House, the brick block of flats on the east side. Number 100 stood here and nothing of it is left; a plaque by the door remembers the fireman Charles Pearson.

stories.title: The siege of Sidney Street
paras: The flats here are called Peter House and Painter House, after a man who was probably never in this street.

On the sixteenth of December 1910 a gang of Latvian revolutionaries, on the run from the Tsar since 1905, are breaking through a wall towards a jeweller's safe in Houndsditch. Police with truncheons knock at the door, and the gang open fire. Sergeants Robert Bentley and Charles Tucker and Constable Walter Choate are killed. Their own man, George Gardstein, is hit too and dies.

On the third of January 1911 an informer says two of them, Fritz Svaars and William Sokoloff, are hiding here, at number 100. At dawn the men open fire with automatic pistols that outgun the police. Scots Guards are called out from the Tower to help the police.

Just before noon the Home Secretary, Winston Churchill, arrives in a top hat. Early in the afternoon the house catches fire, nobody knows how. Churchill backs the police: let it burn. Two bodies are found in the ruins. A falling wall injures the fireman Charles Pearson, and he dies months later.
In the end nobody is convicted. Jacob Peters, Svaars's cousin, goes home to Russia and becomes deputy head of the Cheka, Lenin's secret police. In 1938 Stalin has him shot.

And Peter the Painter? The police called him the ringleader. He was never caught. One historian believes he was Janis Zhaklis, a Latvian militant. Others doubt he was ever at Houndsditch or here, or that he existed at all. The legend got the flats.

stops.name: Wenlock Basin, home
stops.note: Wenlock Basin, and the ride is done. The Eagle is about five minutes away on foot, at the corner of City Road and Shepherdess Walk.

stories.title: In and out the Eagle
paras: One more thing before you put the bike away. A few minutes from this basin, on the corner of City Road and Shepherdess Walk, stands the Eagle.
Up and down the City Road, in and out the Eagle, goes the old song. That's the way the money goes. Pop goes the weasel.

In Victorian London the Eagle is no quiet local. Behind it stands the Grecian, a music hall with gardens, where, the story goes, a fifteen year old Marie Lloyd first sings in public. In the 1880s the Salvation Army buys the lot.
Pop, most people say, meant pawn. What the weasel was, nobody really knows. And that is the end of the ride.
